questions.prompt: What is the chapter's main claim about values?
choices: Values become more real when they claim time on the calendar
Values matter only if they are written in a notebook
Values should never affect planning

explanation.gentle: The chapter turns values into scheduled time.
explanation.direct: Priority becomes more honest when it claims hours.
explanation.competitive: If it matters, it needs the clock.

questions.prompt: Why is the calendar central in this chapter?
choices: Because it reveals what is actually protected in real time
Because it guarantees perfect days
Because it replaces all judgment

explanation.gentle: The calendar shows what the week really defended.
explanation.direct: It makes commitment and tradeoffs visible.

questions.prompt: What does the chapter say to-do lists fail to do well enough?
choices: Force real-time tradeoffs and protected time
Capture any intention at all
Let people remember small tasks

explanation.gentle: Lists collect intentions, but they do not decide where time goes.
explanation.direct: The calendar is stricter because it allocates real hours.
explanation.competitive: The list flatters. The clock forces bids.

questions.prompt: A manager says deep work matters but never blocks time for it. What is the stronger diagnosis?
choices: The value is admired but not yet protected in time
The calendar is irrelevant
Deep work should stay unscheduled

explanation.gentle: The chapter asks where the value lives on the calendar.
explanation.competitive: The value is getting applause and no airtime.

choices: It turns values into visible prior commitments
It guarantees a result
It removes all uncertainty

explanation.gentle: The time block gives the value a place to live.
explanation.direct: Timeboxing makes principle concrete in time.
explanation.competitive: It makes the value sign the contract.

questions.prompt: What question does the calendar force that intention alone does not?
choices: When will this matter in real time, and what will lose that space?
How can I avoid all tradeoffs?
How do I keep every option open forever?

explanation.direct: Real scheduling requires displacement and choice.
explanation.competitive: The clock makes priorities bid against reality.

questions.prompt: What is a key limit of this chapter?
choices: Schedules make priorities visible but do not guarantee perfect control
Scheduling removes the need to revise anything
A calendar proves outcomes are secure

explanation.gentle: The calendar is a tool and test, not magic.
explanation.direct: Commitment can be real without total control.
explanation.competitive: The contract matters even when the day edits itself.

questions.prompt: What makes a value operational instead of sentimental in this chapter?
choices: Protected calendar time
Strong emotion about it
Mentioning it often

explanation.gentle: The chapter wants the value to have a time claim.
explanation.direct: Operational values are scheduled and reviewable.
explanation.competitive: The value has to pay rent in hours.

questions.prompt: How does this chapter change the meaning of traction?
choices: Traction becomes prior intent expressed in time
Traction becomes a feeling of busyness
Traction becomes list length

explanation.gentle: The chapter makes traction visible on the calendar.
explanation.direct: Scheduled prior intent is the new standard of proof.
explanation.competitive: Traction stops being sentiment and starts occupying hours.

questions.prompt: Why does the next chapter move into inputs rather than outcomes?
choices: Because once a value has time, the next question is what part of the work can actually be controlled
Because values no longer matter
Because calendars make outcomes guaranteed

explanation.gentle: The block can be real even when the result is still uncertain.
explanation.direct: The next step is distinguishing controllable effort from uncontrollable result.
explanation.competitive: The hours can be owned before the outcome can.
